extracted.intended_audience: students learning arithmetic (fractions); readers of a historical Italian arithmetic treatise
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and rules (historical/formal) for operating with fractions: definitions of numerators/denominators, how to add, subtract, multiply, divide, compare, reduce, and take parts of quantities expressed as fractions, with geometric/representational remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: How to divide one fraction by another (divisione frazioni).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform division of fractions by transforming the operation into a multiplication by the reciprocal of the divisor: to divide a/b by c/d, multiply a/b by d/c. The text explains splitting and partitioning parts so that the part to be divided is measured in units of the divisor and then multiplied by the reciprocal when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of fractions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply numerators together and denominators together to obtain the product fraction; when convenient, perform cross-cancellation (take parts from numerator and denominator before multiplying) to simplify. The treatise also describes multiplying fractions by whole numbers as repeated addition of the fraction and addresses multiplication across different denominators by aligning units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of fractions / bringing to common denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: How to add fractions (petitio fractjorum / additio fractionum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To add fractions, first make their units (denominators) the same — i.e., find or form a common denominator — then add the numerators. The text emphasizes transforming fractions into comparable parts so the sum is a fraction with a common unit and gives procedural notes about arranging lines/columns of fractions to perform the addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction of fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: How to subtract fractions (subtractionem of fractions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to addition: reduce to a common denominator (same unit) and subtract the numerators. The work discusses ordering, lining up corresponding parts, and handling cases where borrowing or reduction is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing fractions / reducing parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce a fraction or a part by removing common factors (Reducere ad partem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify fractions by dividing numerator and denominator by common factors (reduce to least terms). The treatise advises reducing before or after operations when it makes calculations easier and gives procedural examples of taking out common multiplicative parts to simplify products or quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking a part of a quantity (capere partem)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to take a fractional part of a quantity (finding 'the part' of a given whole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To take a fraction of a quantity, partition the whole into the indicated number of equal parts (the denominator) and take the required number of those parts (the numerator). The section explains extracting parts by partitioning, using tables or alignment of units, and converting mixed quantities into comparable units to take parts correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting multiplication as repeated addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding what multiplication of fractions or numbers means in terms of repeated addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is viewed as adding that fraction to itself the given number of times. The text repeatedly uses this interpretation to justify procedures and to guide computations where a fraction is scaled by an integer multiplier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling whole parts and mixed numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: How to treat fractions that include whole (unit) parts: conversion and alignment with fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When operations involve whole units with fractions, the treatise recommends converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or splitting the whole part into fractional units) so operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication) proceed in the same uniform way. It also suggests keeping track of the whole-unit column separately when aligning for computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding how many times one number is contained in another
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for determining how many units of one number (or fraction) fit into another (division as containment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated subtraction/partitioning, form units so the divisor's unit appears in the dividend, or convert to a common unit and count how many times the divisor's unit is contained. The treatise gives algorithmic steps and examples for integer and fractional containment problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of fractions (which is larger / difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to compare two fractions and determine how much larger one is than the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring the fractions to a common denominator (same unit) and compare numerators. To find the difference, subtract numerators once denominators are equal. The text also offers geometric intuition (lines, surfaces) to justify comparisons of magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of geometric/representational analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting fractions and operations by analogy to lines, surfaces, and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise uses geometry (faces of squares, lengths, areas) as models: e.g., comparing lengths vs. surfaces, explaining how multiplication affects area (product of sides), and using these analogies to make sense of 'more' or 'less' when comparing fractions and numbers. These representations guide whether to compare as lines or surfaces and when such comparisons are meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical notation and unit choice for fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifying what is meant by 'unit' (unità), numerator and denominator, and the effect of different unit choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that fractions are measured with respect to a chosen unit: when units differ, transform to a single unit before operating. It explains that sometimes one can choose a more convenient common unit (e.g., by multiplying numerator/denominator) to simplify operations and highlights mistakes that arise from failing to align units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-multiplication and allocation of parts in products
rubrics_metrics.description: How to handle multiplication of fractions by cross-multiplying parts or taking specified parts of a product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiplying fractions, one may form the multiplication as crossing numerators and denominators (taking parts of the multiplication) so that particular parts of the multiplication represent the desired portion of a product. The method is used both to compute and to pick out particular partial products represented by certain numerators/denominators in the overall multiplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding common multiples / constructing a common denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: How to find or form a common multiple (denominator) for combining fractions or for aligning units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct common denominators by taking multiples of denominators (or their product) so that fractional quantities can be expressed with the same unit; the treatise gives practical guidance on choosing least common multiples where possible and using tables/arrangements to organize the multiples during computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing multi-step fraction computations (tables, lining up parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural guidance to arrange fractional computations (many terms, many factors) to avoid error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place related fractional parts in rows/columns or tables, align like units, and perform repeated addition or multiplication across the organized layout. The text repeatedly recommends arranging 'righe' (rows) and 'tauloletta' (small table) to see how fractions combine and to track multiplications and sums systematically.
